Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing

precontemplation to maintenance · motivational interviewingWhich stage, and which move?

Bottom line
  • Name the stage from what the patient says now: sees no problem, precontemplation; sees a problem but is ambivalent, contemplation; committed and asking how, preparation; changing now, action; keeping the change, maintenance; back to the old habit, relapse
  • The move is motivational interviewing: open-ended, nonjudgmental questions that let the patient explore their own reasons to change; reflect what you hear and do not argue or impose change
  • Match the move to the stage: before commitment, explore the reasons and the ambivalence; once committed, strategies and resources; after the change, plans for coping with temptation (relapse prevention)

The stages describe readiness to change a health behavior such as substance use, diet or exercise; motivational interviewing aims to move the patient through them over time, and relapse does not always happen Where it is usedMotivational interviewing is an evidence-based treatment for alcohol use disorder; it sits beside cognitive-behavioral therapy for stimulant use disorder and is one behavioral intervention for relapse prevention

Stages of change
StageThe patient saysNext move
Precontemplation"My drinking is not the problem; my nerves are." Sees no problem with the habitOpen-ended, nonjudgmental questions about the habit; do not argue
Contemplation"I know it hurts me, but I am not sure I want to stop." Sees a problem, ambivalent about changeExplore the ambivalence: the reasons for and against change, in the patient's own words
Preparation (determination)"I have decided to quit. What can help me?" Committed, asking howDiscuss strategies and resources for the change
Action (willpower)"I have stopped, and it is hard." Taking steps nowAffirm the effort and reflect the talk of change
Maintenance"I have stayed off it and want to keep it that way." Keeping a change already madePlan how to cope with temptation to return to the habit (relapse prevention)
Relapse"I was doing well, then I started again." Back to the old habit after a changeWithout judgment, review what helped and what did not in past attempts
Motivational interviewing moves
MoveWhat it does
Open-ended questionLets the patient tell it in their own words, without being led: "What do you like about drinking, and what worries you about it?"
ReflectionRestates what the patient said as a statement, such as "Part of you wants to stop"; reflect most when you hear talk of change
AffirmationA genuine statement about the patient's strengths, values or efforts
SummaryGathers what the patient said and marks a transition in the conversation
Eliciting the patient's reasonsThe patient, not the physician, voices the arguments for and against change; change is supported, never imposed
Nonjudgmental stanceAccepts ambivalence and tolerates resistance; arguing with the patient works against change
Commonly confused
PairDecides it
Precontemplation or contemplationWhether the patient sees a problem at all: none, precontemplation; a problem but unsure about change, contemplation
Contemplation or preparationUnsure whether to change, or committed and ready to discuss how
Action or maintenanceMaking the change now, or keeping a change already made
Pause point
Drinks daily after five treatment programs; says his drinking will be under control once his anxiety is treated Offered as contemplation, maintenance or relapse prevention Does he see the habit itself as the problem now? → No: he blames his anxiety, so precontemplation; past treatment does not set the stage
Practice
  1. 52-year-old man has had a cough all winter He smokes a pack daily and blames the cough on allergies He quit twice in the past and sees no reason to quit now → Precontemplation → He does not see his smoking as a problem; past quit attempts do not set his stage, which is named from his present view of the habit
  2. 34-year-old woman drinks four or five glasses of wine most nights She says drinking hurts her sleep and her marriage, but it is how she unwinds She is not sure she wants to cut back → Contemplation → She names the harm yet is unsure about change: ambivalence marks contemplation
  3. 46-year-old man with type 2 diabetes returns for a routine visit He says he has decided to start walking after dinner and change his diet He asks which exercise programs his insurance covers → Preparation (determination) → He has committed to change and wants strategies and resources but has not yet begun: preparation
  4. 28-year-old man is treated for a hand fracture from a fight while drunk He says he drinks no more than his friends and has no problem He agrees to talk with the physician before discharge → Ask what he likes about drinking and what, if anything, concerns him → He sees no problem (precontemplation), so motivational interviewing opens with open-ended, nonjudgmental questions that let him voice his own reasons; arguing or imposing a plan works against change
  5. 31-year-old woman who smokes has two young children She says, "I want to quit for my kids, but smoking is the only thing that calms me down." She has not made any plan to quit → "Part of you wants to quit for your children, and part of you relies on smoking to stay calm." → She is ambivalent (contemplation): reflecting both sides in her own words helps her explore the ambivalence, while a quit date fits a patient who is committed to quitting
  6. 50-year-old man who drinks daily says he has decided to stop He asks what could help him stay off alcohol He has no symptoms of withdrawal and wants to begin soon → Discuss strategies and resources for stopping → He has committed and asks how (preparation), so the move is to discuss strategies and resources for the change
  7. 39-year-old woman stopped drinking after an outpatient program Several months later, after a death in the family, she began drinking again She feels ashamed and says that she wants to stop again → Review, without judgment, what helped and what led back to drinking → After relapse, a nonjudgmental review of what helped and what did not guides the next attempt; relapse is common, with up to 70% resuming heavy drinking despite psychosocial treatment
Pairs with Medications for Substance Use Disorders covers the drugs that pair with motivational interviewing in relapse prevention. Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal covers withdrawal and the psychosocial treatment of each substance.
Transferable rule

Name the stage from what the patient says about the habit now; past treatment does not set the stage. Then ask open-ended, nonjudgmental questions that draw out the patient's own reasons to change.
